summary: An appeal to the Internet community to return unused blocks of IP address space to IANA or the delegated registries so they can be reassigned. It is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: If you have a toy you never play with, give it back so someone else can. This asks people to hand back network addresses they are not using.

questions: how to return unused ip address space
why return unused ip prefixes to iana
how did class a addresses work
subtitle: A case for returning unused IP address blocks to preserve routing infrastructure.

tldr.problem: The Internet was running out of usable IPv4 address space and routing tables were growing too fast, risking infrastructure collapse. Many organizations held large blocks of IP addresses they no longer used.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1917 appeals to organizations and providers to return unused IP address blocks to IANA and regional registries so they can be reallocated, and suggests providers help by reclaiming unused space within their customer allocations.
tldr.outcome: This is a Best Current Practice that advocates for address space conservation to extend IPv4 lifetime and control routing table growth.

today: RFC 1917 is a Best Current Practice and has not been obsoleted. It remains relevant guidance for address conservation, though IPv6 deployment has since become the primary solution to address exhaustion.

sections.title: The Address and Routing Crisis
sections.content:
By 1996, the Internet faced two critical problems. First, there were only 232 possible IPv4 addresses, and the supply was finite. Second, the number of routing table entries was doubling every nine months while router capacity only doubled every eighteen months. At this rate, core routers would become unable to function within two to three years.

The problem was made worse by history: the early IANA had assigned large blocks of addresses based on simple requests rather than demonstrated need, and many of those assignments were now dormant. As the Internet grew and previously offline organizations connected, they brought those addresses online, fragmenting the global routing table.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet was running out of room, both in addresses and in routers' memory. Some old addresses no longer in use were suddenly being used again, breaking the system into pieces.

sections.title: Evolution of IP Address Allocation
sections.content:
Early IP addresses were all the same: 8 bits for the network and 24 bits for the host. As the Internet grew, the system evolved into classes. Class A networks (/8 prefixes) used 50% of the address space and were reserved for the largest organizations. Class B networks (/16 prefixes) made up 25%. Class C networks (/24 prefixes) handled the rest.

Subnetting let organizations divide a single network number into smaller pieces for more efficient use. Later, CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) replaced the rigid class system with flexible prefix lengths. A provider given a CIDR block like 192.168/16 (256 Class C networks) could assign individual Class C networks to customers yet advertise only a single route.

CIDR worked well when blocks were kept intact and hierarchical, but problems emerged when customers changed providers and kept their addresses, or when providers failed to aggregate routes correctly.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet's address system evolved from fixed sizes to flexible blocks. The best way to handle this is to keep blocks together, like keeping all houses on one street under one postal code instead of mixing streets.

sections.title: Sources of Wasted Address Space
sections.content:
The RFC identifies several categories of unused allocations. Some organizations made small initial requests and received multiple Class C assignments, then later received Class B assignments when they grew, leaving the original Class Cs unused. Internet service providers distributed blocks to customers based on service level rather than actual need, creating overcapacity. Organizations that had merged or changed structure now held redundant allocations. Many organizations requested addresses for internal TCP/IP networks that would never connect to the Internet, or used Network Address Translation to hide internal networks.

The common pattern: approximately 50,000 networks had been assigned, but only 30-40% of organizations actually had Internet connectivity. As the Internet's popularity soared, dormant sites came online, fragmenting the routing table with previously unannounced address blocks.
sections.plainLanguage: Companies got more address numbers than they needed, either by accident or because they thought they might need them someday. Now those numbers were scattered across the Internet, making routing harder.

sections.title: The Call to Action
sections.content:
The RFC makes direct appeals to three groups. To organizations: return addresses if unused, or if you are only using a small percentage and could renumber relatively easily, give them back. If your internal networks will never reach the Internet or are air-gapped for security, use reserved private address ranges (RFC 1597) instead and return your global assignments.

To providers: actively encourage customers to renumber and release non-CIDR addresses. Work together to aggregate routes and keep CIDR blocks intact. Verify routes being advertised to ensure correct aggregation. For customers using only part of an assigned block, consider whether upper address ranges could be reallocated to other customers without harming the original customer.

To the IANA and registries: when addresses are returned, route them to the appropriate registry to maximize availability and minimize routing loads.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC asks: if you don't need these numbers, give them back. If you can switch to private numbers, do it. Providers should help customers reorganize, and everyone should keep their addresses neatly grouped.

sections.title: Technical Solutions for Providers
sections.content:
The RFC suggests a specific technique for providers with large customers using only part of their allocated space. If organization S holds Class A block 10.0.0.0 and allocates addresses from right to left, provider P (who advertises 10.0.0.0 to the Internet) could offer some of the upper /18 blocks to other customers. This imposes no burden on S if its router supports BGP, yet allows P to serve many small customers without requesting new address blocks.

The RFC cites the "Net 39" experiment (RFC 1797, summarized in RFC 1879) as practical proof this scheme works. The broader message to providers: pursue both customer renumbering and peering agreements to control route growth. Cooperation between providers was described as essential to managing the Internet's future.
sections.plainLanguage: If a big company only uses part of its address block, the provider can carefully hand out the unused parts to other customers while keeping everything aggregated.

sections.title: Returning Address Space
sections.content: The RFC provides concrete instructions for organizations wanting to return addresses. Send a message to Hostmaster@internic.net and iana@isi.edu updating the contact information to mark the block as RESERVED, with the network number being returned and contact details for Joyce Reynolds and Jon Postel at ISI. Other registries have their own forms and processes. As of the RFC's publication, four Class A networks had already been returned to the IANA, representing over 1.5% of IPv4 capacity.
sections.plainLanguage: To give addresses back, send a form to the IANA saying you're done with them. Different registries handle their own returns.
